newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: PNG returns to calm, acting prime minister expected.
newsitem.headline: PNG returns to calm, acting prime minister expected.

text.p: Calm returned to Papua New Guinea and rebellious soldiers were back in their barracks on Thursday after a 10-day crisis defused by the decision of Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan to step aside.
Chan stood down on Wednesday under widespread pressure to quit for his hiring of mercenaries to crush an uprising on copper-rich Bougainville island.
He was back in parliament on Thursday, answering questions at PNG's Westminster-style prime minister's question time.
But cabinet was expected to quickly name an acting prime minister to guide the country through an inquiry into the mercenary deal and towards national elections due in June.

On his last day in office, the urbane Chan took questions on routine matters such as roads and bridges, but was pressed by the opposition into conceding that the $36 million mercenary deal had damaged PNG's international standing.
"We have...created a tremendous amount of tension that I had never envisaged," Chan said of the crisis sparked by the arrival in the South Pacific nation last month of 70 African soldiers.
After a day of celebrations on Wednesday -- soldiers and protesters still had to respect an anti-crime curfew -- Port Moresby returned to normality on Thursday.
Buses were running and shops, businesses and banks were open. Outside parliament house, street cleaners picked up the debris of the protests which finally toppled Chan.

Frontrunner for the post of acting prime minister was former lands minister Albert Kipalan, a career politician and polished parliamentary performer who is deputy leader of Chan's People's Progress Party.
The other favoured candidate was foreign minister Kilroy Genia, a popular, although less experienced parliamentarian.

The inquiry into the mercenary fiasco is due to run from April 1 to April 18 and theoretically Chan could return to office after that in the run-up to elections -- although political analysts said it was unlikely.

Chan, first elected to parliament in 1968 and who has now served two curtailed terms as prime minister, told New Zealand radio he was likely to be a candidate: "I've got no qualm at all standing for the election."
He said he had won a 60 percent majority in his constituency at the last election and hoped to increase that.

Papua New Guinea-linked stocks listed in Australia jumped in early trade on Thursday and analysts said investors were relieved not just that stability had returned but that PNG's democratic institutions had not been damaged.
"Everyone is relieved that the parliamentary process actually worked and that we didn't go into a period of military control," ABN AMRO head of mining research David Walker said.
Orogen Minerals Ltd, which is 51-percent owned by the PNG government, rose 13 cents to A$3.15 (US$2.48), while Oil Search Ltd rose 11 cents to A$2.68 on heavy volume.
Bougainville Copper Ltd, which controls Bougainville's vast abandoned Panguna copper mine and is a unit of mining giant RTZ-CRA, rose five cents to 60 cents.

Chan's mercenaries had been under order to recapture the mine but were forced out of PNG before they could launch an assault. Market analysts said the return to order might, however, facilitate a longer-term solution to the nine-year secessionist rebellion.
